title: Recursion
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of recursion in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply recursion to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Recursion is lesson 51 in Methods and Reusable Code. A method names a unit of behavior, with explicit inputs and an explicit result or side effect. Keep its responsibility narrow and test meaningful edge cases.
content.why_it_matters: Small methods give a program testable units and make intent visible. This lesson focuses on recursion and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A method names a unit of behavior, with explicit inputs and an explicit result or side effect. Keep its responsibility narrow and test meaningful edge cases.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for recursion. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Understanding recursive methods
items.text: For understanding recursive methods, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to recursion, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Base cases
items.text: Design methods around one responsibility, clear inputs, and a clear result. Prefer ordinary value parameters by default; use overloads and modifiers only when they make the contract easier to understand.

items.title: Recursive cases
items.text: For recursive cases, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to recursion, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Direct and indirect recursion
items.text: Design methods around one responsibility, clear inputs, and a clear result. Prefer ordinary value parameters by default; use overloads and modifiers only when they make the contract easier to understand.

items.title: Stack usage and recursive performance
items.text: Select a collection from the operations the caller needs: order, key lookup, uniqueness, FIFO/LIFO, sorted access, concurrency, or immutability. Program against the narrowest useful interface and check equality/hash-code behavior for keys.

content_blocks.text: A method names a unit of behavior, with explicit inputs and an explicit result or side effect. Keep its responsibility narrow and test meaningful edge cases.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates recursion. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates recursion rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for recursion before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
